title: RAW UNREVIEWED: crossed visual-property recombination must preserve independently learned construction roles
summary: RAW_UNREVIEWED_NOT_SELECTED_NOT_TESTED. Jointly constrain complete-word families using independently coded image properties, text-only construction roles, and directed form composition. Learn from three occupied combinations of two visual properties and predict the fourth combination on separate leaves. An apparent image-word association that only names a correlated plant cluster should fail the changed combination even when its training accuracy is high. No particular whole or component receives a meaning in this proposal.

design.mechanism: Crosssituational learning separates reusable property contributions from topic-specific whole-form residues only if grammatical context and crossed image evidence agree.
design.unit: Complete native forms in complete entries, with an independently frozen image-property pair and text-only role inventory; held physical leaves and held property combinations.
design.contrast: Grammar-conditioned reusable property contributions versus atomic whole-word topic model, image-bag-only predictor, and unrestricted family collapse with matched complexity.
design.prediction: The same visual-property contribution predicts a change across more than one lexical family while preserving its text-role distribution; the crossed fourth combination must be predicted without relearning that combination. Atomic whole-form residuals remain allowed and paid.
design.scope: RAW proposal only. GDT1157 is single-image-feature to whole-word occurrence; this is a held-combination interaction with independent grammar constraints. GDT326 unseen combination failure and GDT608 atomic advantage retained, not overwritten. Needs actual replicated crossed image support; no picture-feature absence inferred from unobservability, no pooling readers, no exact parallel paragraph prerequisite. Full word profiles required before discussing specific meanings; source-owned historical semantics would still be needed to distinguish descriptive property from associated use.
